**In Praise of Moss**

Almost nobody looks at moss. We step on it, scrape it off roofs, and treat it as green background, the botanical equivalent of elevator music. But moss may be the most quietly successful thing alive.

Mosses were among the first plants to crawl out of the water, roughly 450 million years ago, long before trees, flowers, or anything with a backbone walked on land. They have no roots, only tiny threads called rhizoids that anchor them without drinking. They have no vascular system to move water. Every cell must fend for itself, absorbing moisture straight from rain and air. By most engineering standards, moss is badly designed. And yet it has outlasted the dinosaurs, several ice ages, and countless species that seemed far better equipped.

Its secret is patience. Many mosses can dry out almost completely, curling into brittle brown tufts that look dead. Then, when water returns, they unfurl and begin photosynthesizing again within hours. Scientists have revived Antarctic moss that had been frozen under ice for over 1,500 years. It simply woke up and kept growing, as if it had only paused.

I find something hopeful in that. We tend to admire strength that looks like force: towering redwoods, charging animals, loud ambition. Moss suggests another model. It survives by being small, adaptable, and willing to wait. It doesn't conquer the forest; it softens it, holding soil, sheltering insects, and turning bare rock into the beginnings of ground.

Next time you pass a mossy stone, consider pausing. You're looking at a very old survivor.
